title: Sudama's handful of rice
word: reading the Isha in the original
hookLine: Krishna eats a poor friend's handful of rice; enjoy by letting go
carry: it's all the Lord's: offer it, then enjoy
tomorrow: where did the word 'here' go in the Isha's second verse?
last: ISHA VASYAM: THE LORD LIVES IN ALL THIS.

lines: A FRIEND WITH NOTHING TO BRING.
cards: Some people show up to a friend's house with a big gift. Some show up with whatever they could find, and feel small at the door.
In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna's old school friend, the one families call Sudama, is that second guest. He's so poor his wife has to borrow a few handfuls of flattened rice for him to bring.
He walks all the way to Krishna's palace, sees the gold, and hides his little bundle.

teach.b: Krishna runs to meet him, washes his feet, and sits him down like family. Then he spots the bundle, pulls it open, and eats a handful of that plain rice with real joy.
Sudama goes home without asking for a thing, and finds his hut has become a house. The rice didn't matter. The offering did.

teach.h: TENA TYAKTENA BHUNJITHA: LET GO, ENJOY.
teach.b: Now the Isha's half-verse: tena tyaktena bhunjitha ma gridhah kasya svid dhanam. Tena tyaktena: by that letting go. Bhunjitha: may you enjoy.
Ma gridhah: don't grasp. Kasya svid dhanam: whose, I wonder, is wealth? The small word svid is a raised eyebrow.
Here's the teaching, and it follows from yesterday.
If the Lord lives in all this, then nothing is finally mine. So many teachers read the line this way: hold what you have as given, let it go, and enjoy it as a gift.

teach.h: OFFER IT, EAT IT AS PRASAD.
teach.b: That's why so many Hindu families offer food to the Lord before anyone eats, and then eat it back as prasad, his gift. In the Gita, Krishna says a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water offered with love is enough.
Sudama's rice was enough. Letting go isn't losing the meal. It's how the meal becomes a gift.

how: Many Hindu families offer food to the deity before eating (naivedya) and then share it as prasad; teachers often explain the Isha's half-line the same way: hold what you have as the Lord's and enjoy it as a gift.

games.q: what does “reading the isha in the original” mean?
o: the Isha's rules for giving away all you own
Krishna asking his friends for expensive gifts
a poor friend's rice, and enjoying what you let go

games.q: three moods in half a verse — tap the pairs.

s: the Isha tells people to give up everything and enjoy nothing
bhunjitha is a wish: may you enjoy, by letting go.
many Hindu families eat food that was first offered to the Lord, and call it prasad
offered first, then received back as his gift, like Sudama's rice.
Krishna turned down Sudama's rice because it was too plain
he ate it with joy: the offering mattered, not the rice.

games.q: Sam is over for dinner and asks why Priya's family puts a plate in front of Krishna's picture before anyone eats. what's the answer?
o: it's all the Lord's, so it's offered first; then the family eats it as prasad, his gift.
the gods are hungry and need to be fed first.
it's for luck, so the food doesn't go bad.
games.why: tena tyaktena bhunjitha: let go, then enjoy. the food is offered first and eaten back as prasad, the way Krishna received Sudama's rice.

practice: Hold something small in an open palm: a sip of water, a piece of fruit, even a pen. If you pray, offer it in your heart, the way families offer food before a meal. If you don't, simply notice it was given to you.
Then, slowly, take it back and enjoy it, as a gift.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Isha in the original, half a verse at a time: let go, may you enjoy, don't grasp, and whose, I wonder, is wealth? Sudama's rice, offered and enjoyed.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: tyaktena, by the given-up, from tyaj, to let go.

carryVoice: Your line: it's all the Lord's: offer it, then enjoy. A handful of rice was enough. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 1, second line (tena tyaktena bhunjitha ma gridhah kasya svid dhanam)
